}}In [[statistics]], the '''matrix variate beta distribution''' is a generalization of the [[beta distribution]]. It is also called the '''[[Multivariate analysis of variance|MANOVA]] ensemble''' and the '''Jacobi ensemble'''.

If <math>U</math> is a <math>p\times p</math> [[positive definite matrix]] with a matrix variate beta distribution, and  <math>a,b>(p-1)/2</math> are real parameters, we write <math>U\sim B_p\left(a,b\right)</math> (sometimes <math>B_p^I\left(a,b\right)</math>).  The [[probability density function]] for <math>U</math> is:<math display="block">
\left\{\beta_p\left(a,b\right)\right\}^{-1}
\det\left(U\right)^{a-(p+1)/2}\det\left(I_p-U\right)^{b-(p+1)/2}.
</math>

Here <math>\beta_p\left(a,b\right)</math> is the [[multivariate beta function]]:

:<math>
\beta_p\left(a,b\right)=\frac{\Gamma_p\left(a\right)\Gamma_p\left(b\right)}{\Gamma_p\left(a+b\right)}
</math>

where <math>\Gamma_p\left(a\right)</math> is the [[multivariate gamma function]] given by

:<math>
\Gamma_p\left(a\right)= \pi^{p(p-1)/4}\prod_{i=1}^p\Gamma\left(a-(i-1)/2\right).
</math>

== Theorems == 

=== Distribution of matrix inverse ===

If <math>U\sim B_p(a,b)</math> then the density of <math>X=U^{-1}</math> is given by

:<math>
\frac{1}{\beta_p\left(a,b\right)}\det(X)^{-(a+b)}\det\left(X-I_p\right)^{b-(p+1)/2}
</math>
provided that <math>X>I_p</math> and <math>a,b>(p-1)/2</math>.

===Orthogonal transform===

If <math>U\sim B_p(a,b)</math> and <math>H</math> is a constant <math>p\times p</math> [[orthogonal matrix]], then <math>HUH^T\sim B(a,b).</math>

Also, if <math>H</math> is a random orthogonal <math>p\times p</math> matrix which is [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] of <math>U</math>, then <math>HUH^T\sim B_p(a,b)</math>, distributed independently of <math>H</math>.

If <math>A</math> is any constant <math>q\times p</math>, <math>q\leq p</math> matrix of [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] <math>q</math>, then <math>AUA^T</math> has a [[generalized matrix variate beta distribution]], specifically <math>AUA^T\sim GB_q\left(a,b;AA^T,0\right)</math>.

===Partitioned matrix results===

If <math>U\sim B_p\left(a,b\right)</math> and we partition <math>U</math> as

:<math>U=\begin{bmatrix}
U_{11} & U_{12}  \\
U_{21} & U_{22} \end{bmatrix}</math>

where <math>U_{11}</math> is <math>p_1\times p_1</math> and <math>U_{22}</math> is <math>p_2\times p_2</math>, then defining the [[Schur complement]] <math>U_{22\cdot 1}</math> as <math> U_{22}-U_{21}{U_{11}}^{-1}U_{12}</math> gives the following results:

* <math>U_{11}</math> is [[independence (probability)|independent]] of <math>U_{22\cdot 1}</math>
* <math>U_{11}\sim B_{p_1}\left(a,b\right)</math>
* <math>U_{22\cdot 1}\sim B_{p_2}\left(a-p_1/2,b\right)</math>
* <math>U_{21}\mid U_{11},U_{22\cdot 1}</math> has an [[inverted matrix variate t distribution]], specifically <math>U_{21}\mid U_{11},U_{22\cdot 1}\sim IT_{p_2,p_1} \left(2b-p+1,0,I_{p_2}-U_{22\cdot 1},U_{11}(I_{p_1}-U_{11})\right).</math>

=== Wishart results===

Mitra proves the following theorem which illustrates a useful property of the matrix variate beta distribution.  Suppose <math>S_1,S_2</math> are independent [[Wishart distribution|Wishart]] <math>p\times p</math> matrices <math>S_1\sim W_p(n_1,\Sigma), S_2\sim W_p(n_2,\Sigma)</math>.  Assume that <math>\Sigma</math> is [[positive definite matrix|positive definite]] and that <math>n_1+n_2\geq p</math>. If

:<math>U = S^{-1/2}S_1\left(S^{-1/2}\right)^T,</math>

where <math>S=S_1+S_2</math>, then <math>U</math> has a matrix variate beta distribution <math>B_p(n_1/2,n_2/2)</math>.  In particular, <math>U</math> is independent of <math>\Sigma</math>.

== Spectral density ==
The spectral density is expressed by a [[Jacobi polynomials|Jacobi polynomial]].<ref>{{Harvard citation|Potters|Bouchaud|2020}}</ref>

=== Extreme value distribution ===
The distribution of the largest eigenvalue is well approximated by a transform of the [[Tracy–Widom distribution]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johnstone |first=Iain M. |date=2008-12-01 |title=Multivariate analysis and Jacobi ensembles: Largest eigenvalue, Tracy–Widom limits and rates of convergence |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-36/issue-6/Multivariate-analysis-and-Jacobi-ensembles--Largest-eigenvalue-TracyWidom-limits/10.1214/08-AOS605.full |journal=The Annals of Statistics |volume=36 |issue=6 |doi=10.1214/08-AOS605 |issn=0090-5364|arxiv=0803.3408 }}</ref>
